Will-o'-the-wisps are still-unexplained transient lights reported by old travelers—they form a big part of European folklore. They’re generally seen to be bad omens; some strains of myth depict them as souls rejected from Hell.

draws a connection with the will-o'-the-wisp in Goethe’s
Faust
In Goethe’s
Faust
(I.xxi), a will-o'-the-wisp lights the way up the “magic-mad” mountain as Faust and Mephistopheles make their way toward the Walpurgisnacht (Witches' Sabbath) assembly. (p.452)

4377583.twitter_share_message:

children: He suffers from Sydenham chorea. Via
Britannica:
Sydenham chorea,
also called
St. Vitus Dance, chorea minor, infectious chorea,
or
rheumatic chorea,

a neurological disorder characterized by irregular and involuntary movements of muscle groups in various parts of the body that follow streptococcal infection. The name St. Vitus Dance derives from the late Middle Ages, when persons with the disease attended the chapels of St. Vitus, who was believed to have curative powers….Most often a manifestation of rheumatic fever, Sydenham chorea occurs most frequently between the ages of 5 and 15 years, and is more common in girls than boys. The disease may occur as an infrequent complication of pregnancy.
St. Vitus' dance is also the term for a medieval
dancing mania,
a bizarre social phenomenon
in which:

…outbreaks seized groups of people who engaged in frenzied dancing that lasted intermittently for days or weeks. Social scientists typify victims as females who were maladjusted, deviant, irrational, or mentally disturbed. These activities were typically accompanied by symptoms similar to tarantism, including screaming, hallucinations, convulsive movements, chest pains, hyperventilation, crude sexual gestures and outright intercourse. Instead of spider bites as the cause, participants usually claimed that they were possessed by demons who had induced an uncontrollable urge to dance.
The causes are still not fully understood; however the
Skeptical Inquirer

argues that religious sects (not disease or “hysteria”) were probably responsible, and that many “facts” about the dancing manias (that they were spontaneous, mostly sustained by women, etc.) don’t hold up to scrutiny.
Medieval dance crazes: truly crazy.

8726463.fragment: Grab wafers between which are wedged lumps of coal and copper snow

range.content: grab wafers between which are wedged lumps of coal and copper snow

8726463.twitter_share_message: “This whole episode is a wild and weird Witches Sabbath, and its phantasmagorical method makes it…” —@Genius

children: This whole episode is a wild and weird Witches Sabbath, and its phantasmagorical method makes it difficult to maneuver. The initial scene has us guessing at what it is we’re looking at when the narrator describes a cart owned by the “real” Antoni Rabaiotti dispensing ice cream, surrounded by squabbling “stunted” men and women, who greedily “grab wafers between which are wedged lumps of coal and copper snow.” They’re all “children,” the narrator explains. The immediately available choices for interpretation are, of course, many and diverse: Are the figures children who are “stunted” future adults? Are they merely callow adults acting immaturely? A deeper search by the reader will reveal that this first scene hearkens back to the
Wandering Rocks
episode, where children are eating ice cream by Rabaiotti’s ice cream cart when they encounter a one-legged sailor who “growls” at them. That he is a sailor is why the children order him to salute.

Of course, nothing has to make sense in this surreal setting, but, since Joyce is not one to “waste” his imagery, a carnival atmosphere such as this at the gateway to the carnal, when the root of “carnival” is
carne vale
, or “farewell to flesh,” with
vale

representing a Latin “good-bye” (literally “be strong” or “be well”), it is difficult not to see this as yet one more jab at Irish lechery-born paralysis, especially when, after clamoring for the ice cream, and having sucked on what turns out to be lumps of coal and copper snow, the children “scatter slowly” in apparent chagrin.
What we will encounter repeatedly in
Circe
are glimpses into past passages in the book that now take on completely different understandings – epiphanies. This chapter is about sudden enlightenment – epiphany (among other things).

children: Mercurous chloride (Hg2Cl2) is also known as calomel. Strangely, it was a white compound ! It was a popular drug from the 1800s onwards as it contained mercury, a chemical that was claimed to cure many illnesses. However, it slowly poisoned those who used it because mercury is toxic. James Joyce: The author of Ulysses developed syphilis in 1904 after visiting “Nighttown” in Dublin. Joyce’s father also may have had syphilis. Joyce had an iridectomy to enlarge his tiny fixed pupil.

Joyce’s syphilis was not reported by the otherwise candid Stanislaus Joyce (Dr. J McCourt   The Years of Bloom, James Joyce in Trieste 1904-1920)!

The name’s slightly senile, but if that’s too much of a mouthful, you can call me one or the other. You could call me “that guy” for all I care. I’ve been on the site since around late 2016. @ewokABdevito began mentoring me for editorship in about June 2017 and I was made an editor in September the same year. Speaking of which, if I ever reject one of your annotations or you just need general help with something, feel free to DM (direct message) me.

I like to think of myself as a jack-of-all-trades, since I’ve written tates for just about everything. That includes new hip-hop, old hip-hop, indie hip-hop, instrumental hip-hop, musical theater, operettas, literature, philosophy, poetry, satirical opinion articles, old jazz standards, the Bible, folk music, the Constitution, the Magna Carta, new wave punk, stand-up routines, mock scripts, theme songs, theme park attractions, and some indie rock here and there. children: See too the
Keats poem of the same name
O what can ail thee, knight-at-arms,
Alone and palely loitering?
The sedge has withered from the lake,
And no birds sing.
O what can ail thee, knight-at-arms,
So haggard and so woe-begone?
The squirrel’s granary is full,
And the harvest’s done.
I see a lily on thy brow,
With anguish moist and fever-dew,
And on thy cheeks a fading rose
Fast withereth too.
I met a lady in the meads,
Full beautiful, a fairy’s child;
Her hair was long, her foot was light,
And her eyes were wild.
I made a garland for her head,
And bracelets too, and fragrant zone;
She looked at me as she did love,
And made sweet moan
I set her on my pacing steed,
And nothing else saw all day long,
For sidelong would she bend, and sing
A faery’s song.
She found me roots of relish sweet,
And honey wild, and manna-dew,
And sure in language strange she said—
‘I love thee true’.
She took me to her Elfin grot,
And there she wept and sighed full sore,
And there I shut her wild, wild eyes
With kisses four.
And there she lullèd me asleep,
And there I dreamed—Ah! woe betide!—
The latest dream I ever dreamt
On the cold hill side.
I saw pale kings and princes too,
Pale warriors, death-pale were they all;
They cried—‘La Belle Dame sans Merci
Hath thee in thrall!’
I saw their starved lips in the gloam,
With horrid warning gapèd wide,
And I awoke and found me here,
On the cold hill’s side.
And this is why I sojourn here,
Alone and palely loitering,
Though the sedge is withered from the lake,
And no birds sing.
